rules.explanation: Hard Law of the Kitchen: A map projection cannot be conformal AND equal-area at the same time. Preserving local angular relationships requires stretching scale equally in all directions (a = b), while preserving relative area requires the product of scale factors to equal unity (a · b = 1). When shapes distort to preserve area, angles must bend. You must choose whether shape or area matters most.

Clashing Dish: Using a global conformal projection (like Mercator) for thematic choropleth maps misleads readers severely by exaggerating high-latitude land areas (Greenland appears the size of Africa when Africa is actually 14x larger). For global statistics or choropleths, an equal-area recipe is essential.

Clashing Dish: Conic projections place the apex of the cone beyond the pole, producing severe convergence and distortion at extreme polar latitudes. For polar regions, planar (azimuthal) projections centered on the pole provide natural circular symmetry and minimum distortion.
Clashing Dish: Conic surfaces cannot wrap effectively around the equator without degenerating into an infinitely tall cone. Cylindrical projections are far better matched to equatorial bands.
Clashing Dish: Normal cylindrical projections stretch meridians infinitely (Mercator) or compress parallels to extreme slivers at the poles. Never serve a polar map on a normal cylinder.

Great Dish: Albers Equal-Area Conic is the gold-standard recipe for mid-latitude countries with predominantly east-west extent (such as the United States or Central Europe). True area is maintained everywhere, with near-zero angular distortion between standard parallels.

Great Dish: Lambert Conformal Conic is the premier choice for mid-latitude aviation charts, meteorological mapping, and state coordinate systems (SPCS). True local shapes and angles are impeccably preserved across broad east-west corridors.

Great Dish: Azimuthal projections in polar aspect provide an unobstructed, circular view of sea ice, polar routes, and cryosphere dynamics. Direction from the pole is true along every straight meridian.

Great Dish: Universal Transverse Mercator (UTM) or Transverse Mercator is the engineering industry benchmark. Secant cylinder geometry keeps scale distortion under 0.04% to 0.1% within each 6° zone, making it ideal for cadastral surveying and engineering.

Great Dish: Pseudocylindrical projections like Mollweide or Eckert IV preserve proportional geographic areas across all continents while curving outer meridians gently to avoid the severe shearing seen in rectangular cylindrical maps.

Great Dish: Winkel Tripel and Robinson are time-tested compromise projections (used by National Geographic) that balance area and angular distortions simultaneously, yielding a visually graceful and natural-looking global atlas plate.
Great Dish: Azimuthal Equidistant preserves both true bearing and true distance from its center point to every other location on the planet (famously featured on the United Nations emblem).
